transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE); Marcus Lee (Redwood SE); Jin Park (Redwood Solutions Eng); Ravi Patel (HelixAI - Head of ML); Sofia Gomez (HelixAI - Infra); Liam Chen (HelixAI - MLOps); Aisha Khan (HelixAI - Security)

Summary (auto):
High-level technical deep-dive focused on model-specific tuning for Llama, Mistral and Qwen families. Discussed MoE routing overhead, rope scaling artifacts, KV cache strategies, batching/throughput tradeoffs, quantization effects on latency/quality, and VPC/on-prem implications for HelixAI's PoC. Agreed next steps to run targeted benchmarks, share security pack, and schedule on-prem pilot.

Topics: model tuning, KV cache, batching, quantization, MoE routing costs, rope scaling, VPC/on-prem deployment, benchmarking

Action items (brief): Marcus to run benchmarks; Sofia to share infra topology; Elena to send security docs; Ravi to finalize SLAs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Elena Park: okay hey everyone thanks for hopping on. um the plan for today is a deep-dive into tuning for the Llama/Mistral/Qwen families, plus how that maps to your vpc and on-prem constraints. Marcus will run most of the benchmarks context.
[00:18] Ravi Patel: thanks elena, yeah our goal is to validate both hosted-like latency and on-prem throughput for our retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, we want 200ms p95 for 8k context ideally but we'll trade for cost if needed.
[00:35] Marcus Lee: yep, good to call that out early. also want to flag MoE models — if you evaluate Mistral-MoE variants there is an additional routing cost that shows up as spikes if you don't shard properly.
[00:50] Sofia Gomez: when you say routing cost you mean intra-node all-reduce or the CPU-based gating? we've seen gating saturate CPUs on our current k8s nodes.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: both, right now routing has two components — the expert selection/gate which can be CPU-heavy if done on CPU and the expert activation that causes memory movement. on a single node with multiple experts you can end up with memory copy overhead and PCIe transfers that spike latency. our runtime supports GPU-side gating for some kernels which reduces the CPU bottleneck but requires certain kernel builds and cuda versions.
[01:30] Jin Park: also interesting is the tradeoff with quantization there — some MoE paths don't quantize as well and you can see quality regressions if you do 4-bit across experts without per-expert calibration.
[01:45] Liam Chen: quick question — for Qwen family models, what have you seen for kv-cache efficiency? our workload has lots of short-turn dialogs so cache hitrate matters.
[02:00] Marcus Lee: Qwen's attention and rope scaling behaves slightly differently than Llama; the position embeddings (rope) scaling can cause drift in long contexts if you downsample or rescale incorrectly. for short turn dialogs kv-cache hit rate is mostly affected by request routing and prompt prefix normalization; make sure tokens are normalized across callers or you lose cache.
[02:25] Ravi Patel: hmm ok. Sofia, our infra currently has A100s with 80GB and some older A40s. we were planning to try qwen-34b on a single 80GB to test latency. is that realistic?
[02:40] Sofia Gomez: yeah we can get a node, question is whether we should use dedicated or run on our shared cluster with taints. we worry about noisy neighbors for latency-sensitive p95.
[02:55] Marcus Lee: for a clean latency test you want a dedicated GPU with pinned processes; shared clusters give good throughput but p95 suffers. on qwen-34b single-node we typically see ~180-240ms p50 for 1k tokens with continuous batching off, p95 depends on network and host config though.
[03:20] Elena Park: and if you enable batch padding/configured batching you can get better amortized cost but p95 will increase if you allow larger batches to wait. so it's a knob.
[03:35] [00:03:40] Ravi Patel: we care about tail — our SLA must commit p95 <= 250ms for the first pilots.
[03:45] Marcus Lee: then the baseline is dedicated 80GB with kernel X (we'll capture exact docker runtime/Lib versions). we'll run qwen-34b quantized int8 and also bf16 to compare quality/latency.
[04:00] Jin Park: we should also run with and without prefix/KV cache enabled to see impact on throughput. logic: with caching you reduce compute per token heavily but need more memory for KV.
[04:18] Liam Chen: what about KV cache eviction policies? our sessions have many users so cache memory is constrained.
[04:28] Marcus Lee: you can do LRU-like trimming by token-length or prioritize active sessions; Redwood runtime supports per-route kv cache configs and TTLs, we can simulate your session churn during the benchmark.
[04:45] Sofia Gomez: does that require zookeeper/redis? we prefer not to add external state.
[04:52] Marcus Lee: no, cache is in-process or local shared memory on node; for cross-node warm cache you can use a lightweight redis but many customers run in-node caches for lowest latency.
[05:05] Ravi Patel: okay great. on the topic of rope scaling — we've seen hallucination drift at longer contexts with Llama-2. is that expected behavior?
[05:18] Marcus Lee: yep rope scaling (rotary position embeddings) interacts with sequence length normalization and precision. When you change model chunking or quantization you can see phase-shifts in older tokens. for Llama variants we sometimes recommend linear rope rescaling during fine-tune or use relative position biases where available.
[05:40] Jin Park: Mistral seems more robust to rope scaling in our internal tests but it depends on the tokenization and the downstream evals.
[05:50] Aisha Khan: from security perspective if we run on-prem we need KMS integration and HSM options, plus audit logs for KV cache access. can redwood support that?
[06:02] Elena Park: yes — Redwood Private supports customer KMS integration, HSM via vendor connectors, and audit logs with per-request metadata. we'll send the security pack that covers SOC2, ISO artifacts, and the audit log schema.
[06:20] Aisha Khan: and SSO? we need SAML with SCIM provisioning.
[06:25] Elena Park: supported. plus RBAC and route-level token scoping for separating test versus prod.
[06:33] Ravi Patel: back to MoE: you mentioned GPU-side gating. what are the practical constraints for enabling that?
[06:42] Marcus Lee: GPU-side gating requires a custom kernel and matching CUDA/driver; we have validated builds for 11.8 and 12.x on certain drivers. also you need sufficient shared memory for per-expert activations. it's not a drop-in for all MoE models but for many Mistral-MoE builds we have it working and it reduces CPU latency by ~40% on our samples.
[07:05] Sofia Gomez: what about network egress during expert activation if experts live on different devices?
[07:12] Marcus Lee: that's the big one — cross-device expert placement drives PCIe/NVLink transfers; we recommend expert sharding aligned to device topology and, if possible, place frequently co-accessed experts on the same device. Redwood's scheduler can co-locate experts by affinity but that assumes dedicated nodes or pinned pools.
[07:35] Ravi Patel: for our PoC we probably want dedicated pools then.
[07:40] Elena Park: agreed. dedicated pools give you predictable tail latency which looks like your priority.
[07:47] [00:07:50] Liam Chen: any tips for quantization configs for Mistral vs Llama vs Qwen? we've tried q8_0 and saw a small perf boost but quality loss on few-shot prompts.
[08:02] Marcus Lee: yeah quantization is model-specific. Llama tends to tolerate 4-bit with per-channel quantization and calibration; Mistral often needs per-layer tuning, and Qwen sometimes needs k-means style post-training quant to avoid bias shifts. for PoC we'll recommend calibrated 4-bit for throughput tests, plus int8 for latency if GPU supports fast int8 kernels. we will include recommended bit-width and per-layer knobs in the benchmark sheet.
[08:30] Jin Park: also watch out for mixed-precision artifacts with rope — quantizing position convs incorrectly can amplify drift.
[08:40] Sofia Gomez: our current cluster uses NCCL 2.18 and CUDA 11.8, will that be OK?
[08:48] Marcus Lee: yes that's one of our validated stacks. we'll still need to match driver minor versions for certain optimized kernels. we'll capture the exact matrix in the doc.
[08:58] Ravi Patel: any data on throughput scaling with batch size for Qwen-34B? we need to find sweet spot for latency vs cost.
[09:08] Marcus Lee: rough rules of thumb — single-request p50 is low on dedicated 80GB, but throughput per GPU increases almost linearly until memory saturation. with dynamic batching you get good tokens/sec but p95 climbs. we typically run a sweep for batch sizes {1,2,4,8,16} and measure tail. For Qwen-34B int8 you might see 1k token/s at batch 8 depending on batch compaction and padding. we'll provide real numbers from the run.
[09:38] Jin Park: and continuous batching in the runtime can hide client variance but you must tune max_wait_time and max_batch_size.
[09:47] Liam Chen: for our RAG use-case max latency 250ms p95 needs small max_wait_time.
[09:53] Marcus Lee: right, set max_wait_time around 5-10ms and keep max_batch_size small for tight SLAs. that reduces batching efficiency but keeps tail down.
[10:05] Sonia: (not present)
[10:08] Aisha Khan: when we go on-prem what's the recommended network topology (eg single node vs multi-node with NVLink)?
[10:17] Marcus Lee: for low-latency single-model inference single-node with NVLink-attached GPUs is best. for high-throughput multi-model or MoE you'd want an NVLink/NVSwitch cluster or DGX-like topology to minimize cross-device copies. if you can't get NVLink, ensure high PCIe bandwidth and isolate network to reduce contention.
[10:38] Ravi Patel: let's talk cost tradeoffs. if we pick dedicated 1x80GB vs 2x40GBs (sharded), how does that affect MoE routing and rope scaling?
[10:50] Marcus Lee: sharded multi-device introduces more cross-device communication which exacerbates MoE routing costs and rope synchronization. rope scaling is orthogonal but multi-device may require careful sequence-chunking to maintain position consistency. generally, a single larger memory device simplifies KV cache and reduces PCIe churn, but has less aggregate compute if you need >1 device.
[11:15] Sofia Gomez: can Redwood's runtime do automatic fallback to smaller model when dedicated pool is saturated?
[11:22] Elena Park: yes, we support smart routing/fallback policies — route by latency/cost/region and fallback to compatible model variants automatically. we'll show config examples in the playbook.
[11:34] Ravi Patel: ok good. Marcus, can you outline the benchmark plan you'll run for us?
[11:40] Marcus Lee: sure: 1) baseline latency p50/p95 p999 with bf16 and int8 for Qwen-34B on a dedicated 80GB; 2) sweep batch sizes and max_wait_time to find latency/cost sweet spot; 3) run MoE Mistral variant with GPU-side gating vs CPU gating to show delta; 4) KV cache on vs off and cache trimming sim for session churn; 5) rope-scaling sensitivity test by increasing context lengths (1k/8k/32k) and measuring drift in perplexity/ems metrics. we'll upload raw logs and perf counters.
[12:16] Aisha Khan: for the on-prem pilot we will need the SOW and security checklist. Elena you'll send those?
[12:23] Elena Park: yes I'll draft SOW and attach security checklist, plus the SOC2/ISO pack.
[12:30] Ravi Patel: can you also include an example RBAC policy for dev vs prod routes?
[12:34] Elena Park: yep, included.
[12:36] Liam Chen: what's the expected timeline to get meaningful numbers? two weeks?
[12:41] Marcus Lee: baseline runs can be done in 2-3 business days if infra is provisioned; the full sweep and MoE runs take up to 10 business days. given holidays we'll aim to deliver initial numbers by 2026-12-24.
[12:58] Sofia Gomez: quick networking Q: for cross-node KV sharing do you recommend RDMA?
[13:05] Marcus Lee: RDMA helps for cross-node KV but introduces complexity; most customers keep KV local and accept slight cold-starts rather than maintain hot global KV over RDMA.
[13:20] Ravi Patel: any gotchas for running this in a VPC with restrictive egress? we have strict egress rules due to compliance.
[13:28] Elena Park: Redwood Private supports air-gapped or restricted egress setups; control plane can be customer-hosted and the inference plane can be fully internal. we'll discuss the connection models in the security pack.
[13:42] Aisha Khan: how about audit logs — can we retain logs for 12 months on-prem?
[13:47] Elena Park: yes, retention and export policies are configurable; we can ship logs to your SIEM or S3-like endpoints on-prem.
[13:58] Jin Park: small nuance — when you tune quantization for Qwen, we recommend running calibration with samples from your actual prompt distributions; please share a ~1k prompt sample set if possible.
[14:12] Ravi Patel: we can do that, we'll prepare anonymized sample prompts.
[14:18] Marcus Lee: great. I'll also test two fallback strategies: model variant fallback and region fallback to see tail behavior under load.
[14:28] Sofia Gomez: for the on-prem pilot who will own day-2 ops? Helix or Redwood?
[14:34] Elena Park: we recommend a handshake: Helix runs infra ops, Redwood supports the runtime and provides runbooks and an optional managed ops add-on. we can include a runbook and an optional ops SLA in the SOW.
[14:50] Ravi Patel: sounds good. any other questions from the team?
[14:55] Aisha Khan: none here.
[14:58] Liam Chen: one more — do you support model partitioning for >80k contexts? we might want to evaluate 64k+ token use.
[15:07] Marcus Lee: yes, we support chunked attention with offload to host memory and streaming KV; for very long contexts you pay in memory and latency, but it's supported. rope/position handling needs careful alignment — we'll include config and recommended chunk sizes.
[15:28] Elena Park: ok let's recap next steps.
[15:31] Elena Park: Marcus will run the benchmarks and share results by 12/24. Sofia will share infra inventory by 12/21. I'll send security pack and SOW by 12/20. Ravi to finalize SLA metrics by 12/22. Helix to share anonymized prompt corpus.
[15:48] Ravi Patel: agreed.
[15:50] Elena Park: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in threads and upload the benchmark sheet.
[15:56] Meeting ends
